KEY MESSAGE 1...

In the mid/upper-levels, a split-flow regime encompasses the U.S., 
with cyclonic flow present over the CWA, as a positively-tilted, 
shortwave trough pivots across the Great Lakes region. Farther 
south, the leading edge of the southern-stream 300 mb jetlet was 
nosing into the Mid-Atlantic region, and was orthogonally-oriented
to a mid-level cold front arcing southward from a deepening cyclone 
located in central Quebec that extended to the Gulf Coast. The net 
result of the associated belt of moist, isentropic ascent along the 
pre-frontal warm-conveyor has maintained a shield of light rain 
across the Ohio River Valley that will continue to move eastward 
throughout the next 24 hours. A deck of low-level stratus also 
trails the rain shield, with the back edge of the deck located 
across central IN and central KY.

At the surface, the demarcation of the synoptic cold front was along 
a line from CLE-CMH-LEX-BWG, with breezy, northwesterly winds 
trailing the front. Shallow convection along this front will yield 
only light rain showers as it moves across the CWA this morning and 
into the early afternoon, and the front will clear east of the CWA 
by about 17-18Z. Following the cessation of rain, low stratus will 
be slow to erode across the eastern half of the CWA; however, full 
insolation will occur prior to sunset for most locations west of the 
I-79 and HWY-119 corridors. High temperatures for this afternoon 
were lowered slightly from the previous forecast(s), especially in 
the higher terrain, as low-level nimbostratus/stratus is expected to 
linger through dusk. Temporary reductions to visibilities will 
accompany the rain today, with the lowest visibilities from light 
fog/mist up in the mountains. 

As the base of the trough passes to the north of the CWA tonight, 
clouds will clear, and temperatures will crater into the middle 20s 
for most of the CWA as the eastern periphery of a 1034 mb polar 
surface high, which is currently located over the north-central 
Great Plains, expands eastward. Some locales in the northeastern 
mountains of may observe low temperatures near 20 degrees or 
possibly the upper teens Tuesday morning, along with wind gusts 
between 15-20 mph due to the maintenance of cross-barrier flow aloft 
on the backside of the departing trough. Shortwave ridging is then 
forecast to shift eastward over the region Tuesday, with the polar 
surface high continuing to strengthen as it rotates towards the 
Adirondack Mountains. The superposition of the anticyclone relative 
to the CWA will maintain a sharp warm nose aloft, thereby shunting 
vertical mixing heights and keeping high temperatures Tuesday in the 
middle-upper 40s for most locales while the northeastern mountains 
struggle to climb out of the middle 30s. Locally gusty winds will 
maintained across the mountains as the polar high strengthens and 
the boundary-layer decouples Tuesday night, with winds transitioning 
towards the east overnight into Wednesday. The effects of adiabatic 
compression from the downslope component to the winds Wednesday will 
yield daytime highs about 10 degrees warmer than the prior day 
across the lowlands while remaining chilly in the mountains.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

Active weather continues to be forecast on Thanksgiving and into 
Friday night. By Wednesday night, the split-flow regime across the 
U.S. will be maintained by a high-frequency wave train originating 
from the far northeastern Pacific Ocean. A vorticity lobe currently 
shearing off of a deamplifying shortwave trough over the Pacific 
Northwest is forecast to dive southeastward into the central Great 
Plains and phase with a southern-stream, shortwave trough pivoting 
into the Deep South during the day Wednesday. As these two features 
begin to phase into a larger-scale trough, the vorticity lobe will 
serve as the impetus for the development of a closed, mid-level low; 
and there are indications of the vortex extending through 200 mb as 
the phasing completes. Subgeostrophic flow through the base of the 
trough in proximity to the northern edge of the southern-stream jet 
streak, which will lose its zonal characteristics via upstream 
troughing over Baja Sur, is forecast to result in the development of 
an amplified, negatively-tilted trough over the region that will 
eject towards New England by Friday. 

The resultant increase in DPVA and moist, isentropic ascent over a 
broad corridor (i.e., the entire Eastern Seaboard) as the attendant 
surface low deepens off of the Atlantic Coast will yield in the 
development of a large, baroclinic leaf as the system phases and 
begins to move poleward. Widespread rainfall is forecast to envelope 
the entire CWA during the predawn hours on Thanksgiving, along with 
breezy, northeasterly winds given the strengthening isallobaric 
response from the deepening surface low. A cold rain is forecast
